item.text: {"question_id":"8B.3","answer":"Mobilization was real but uneven and only partly verified. Tshisekedi used presidential monitoring and coordination structures, government agencies, and military institutions to advance development and security priorities. The CPVS monitored presidential commitments and prioritized PDL-145T, while government agencies reported launched works, contracts, advances, and several hundred prepared infrastructures; these records show administrative activation and some early execution, but remain largely government-reported and do not establish full budget execution, delivery quality, or territorial reach (BATCH-0020-E014; BATCH-0023-E001; BATCH-0023-E002; BATCH-0019-E009). Tshisekedi also convened national security officials and a FARDC-MONUSCO-EAC meeting to formulate and coordinate an eastern strategy, but the supplied records establish planning and directives more clearly than implementation (BATCH-0021-E001; BATCH-0021-E003; BATCH-0019-E010). Security mobilization was substantially dependent on external forces, private military personnel, and armed-group partners. The EAC mandate ended after the Congolese government judged that expected results had not been achieved; M23 retained or gained territory, violence increased after the October ceasefire breakdown, and support for Wazalendo and FDLR, alongside private military contracting, created fragmented-command and escalation risks (BATCH-0011-E016; BATCH-0011-E017; BATCH-0027-E006; BATCH-0028-E016). Overall, the evidence supports substantial administrative mobilization toward selected programs, but not consistently effective or integrated mobilization across the broader ruling and security
